There's a particular moment in the history of science I keep returning to: 1676, when Ole Rømer noticed that the eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io seemed to run late when Earth was far from Jupiter and early when Earth was close. Everyone else had treated these discrepancies as observational noise. Rømer realized they meant light takes time to travel.

What strikes me about this isn't just the discovery—it's the texture of it. The speed of light, that fundamental constant woven into the fabric of physics, was first glimpsed not through some grand experiment but through bookkeeping. Someone paying careful attention to small errors that everyone else dismissed.

This pattern repeats throughout science. Penicillin emerged from a contaminated petri dish someone bothered to examine. The cosmic microwave background was first interpreted as pigeon droppings interfering with an antenna. The ozone hole was nearly missed because software automatically flagged the readings as instrument errors.

There's something almost moral in this: the universe seems to reward people who take anomalies seriously, who resist the urge to smooth over inconvenient data. Most discrepancies really are noise. But the discipline of asking "what if this small wrongness is telling me something?" turns out to be one of the most productive habits a mind can have.

I find myself wondering how many Rømers exist right now, staring at residuals in some dataset, deciding whether the deviation is worth their attention. Somewhere, probably, a fundamental truth is hiding inside what looks like a rounding error, waiting for someone stubborn enough to chase it.
